questions.learningObjective: Apply bayesian inference to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: With 0.1 and 0.71 as the stated parameters, a disease has prevalence 0.1. A test detects it with sensitivity 0.71 when present and has specificity 0.78 when absent. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability, to four decimals, that this person actually has the disease?

options.misconception: Reports only the joint numerator, unnormalized
Reports the prior probability of disease
Reports sensitivity and ignores the base rate

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem gives P(D|+) = se*p / (se*p + (1 - sp)*(1 - p)) = 0.071 / (0.071 + 0.198) = 0.2639. The numerator alone is not a probability because it is unnormalized, and the sensitivity or the prior each ignore the false-positive contributions and the base rate, which is precisely the base-rate fallacy.
questions.hint: Compute true positives and false positives over a population, then take the true-positive share.

What is the joint probability P(A and B), to four decimals?

Computes the marginal probability of the child instead
Uses the conditional probability of the wrong parent state

Undetermined without knowing Q and R together.
options.misconception: Wrongly claims the truth value cannot be evaluated.

options.misconception: Wrongly ties the value to R rather than to the disjuncts.

options.text: Both precision and recall rise together.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the two metrics move in the same direction.

Adds the misplacement penalty rather than subtracting it
Treats delay cost as a reward instead of a penalty

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.
Partially observable, stochastic, static, continuous.

Uses the area of the rectangle instead of step distance
Undercounts by assuming the goal square needs no move

options.misconception: Assumes MIN chooses at the root
Assumes MAX gets to pick a leaf directly
Swaps the roles of MAX and MIN at the two levels

questions.explanation: Minimax backs up values from the leaves. Each MIN child takes the smaller of its leaves, giving 4 and 8. The MAX root then takes the larger of those, 8. Taking maxima at the MIN level swaps the players, while taking a global maximum or minimum ignores the alternating levels entirely, so each of those answers misapplies the recurrence.

options.misconception: Wrongly claims a bound alone searches the space.

Monotone: its value never decreases along a path.
options.misconception: Wrongly states the opposite of the usual monotonicity direction.

options.misconception: Wrongly names the stronger arcwise condition.

questions.stem: Working from 0.18, 0.81, and 0.94, a disease has prevalence 0.18. A test detects it with sensitivity 0.81 when present and has specificity 0.94 when absent. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability, to four decimals, that this person actually has the disease?

Reports the prior probability of disease
Reports sensitivity and ignores the base rate

Computes the marginal probability of the child instead
Uses the conditional probability of the wrong parent state

questions.learningObjective: Apply activation functions to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the small sampling procedure below, a classifier returns the reported scores. An activation function receives input x = -0.5. For the hyperbolic tangent (tanh), what is the activation value at this input, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, showing the key step.

options.misconception: Returns the identity instead of a bounded activation
Flips the sign of the input
Uses the sigmoid, whose range is zero to one

questions.explanation: Evaluating the hyperbolic tangent (tanh) at -0.5 gives -0.4621. Each alternative corresponds to a different function or a sign/clipping mistake: swapping a sigmoid for tanh changes the range, reversing an exponent sign inverts a sigmoid, and forgetting rectification lets negative values pass through a ReLU. Only the correct function and argument yield -0.4621.
questions.hint: Recall the definition and output range of the hyperbolic tangent (tanh), then substitute x.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply network architecture to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: A fully connected (dense) neural layer receives 20 inputs and has 7 output units, with one bias term per output unit. How many trainable parameters does the layer have? Give the exact answer.

options.misconception: Adds a spurious bias row and column
Adds rather than multiplies inputs and units
Omits the bias connections to each unit

questions.explanation: Each of the 7 output units has 20 incoming weights plus one bias, so the layer has (20 + 1) * 7 = 147 trainable parameters. Omitting biases drops one per unit, adding rather than multiplying miscounts the weight matrix, and adding a bias column overcounts by an entire row of weights.
questions.hint: Count weights plus one bias for each output unit.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply convolutional networks to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: With the data 38 / 5 / 2 in view, a convolution operates on an input of spatial size 38 with a filter of size 5, padding P = 2 on each side, and stride S = 1. Using the standard integer floor formula, what is the output spatial size? Give the exact answer, using only the information above.

options.misconception: Off-by-one: forgets the leading output position
Assumes unit stride and no padding
Ignores the zero-padding term

questions.explanation: The output size is floor((W - F + 2P)/S) + 1 = floor((38 - 5 + 4)/1) + 1 = 38. Dropping padding, assuming stride one with no padding, or omitting the final plus one each changes the counted positions and gives a wrong dimension.
questions.hint: Apply floor((W - F + 2P)/S) and remember the leading one.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply value functions to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: The case uses 10, 11 and 0.9; in a Q-learning update, taking action a in state s yields an immediate reward of 10 and leads to state s'. From s' the best action has Q-value 11 (the two successor Q-values are 11 and 11), and the discount factor is gamma = 0.9. What is the target value r + gamma * max Q(s', a'), to four decimals?

options.misconception: Sums successor values instead of taking the maximum
Forgets to discount the future value
Uses the first successor value instead of the maximum

questions.explanation: The one-step target is r + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a') = 10 + 0.9 * 11 = 19.9. Using one successor value ignores the maximization, dropping the discount fails to reduce future rewards, and summing successors double-counts the future. The Bellman optimality target requires exactly the maximum of the successor values.
questions.hint: Take the largest successor Q-value, discount it, and add the immediate reward.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply returns and discounting to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: An agent receives rewards 8, 4, 8 at three successive time steps with discount factor gamma = 0.9. What is the discounted return G0 = r0 + gamma*r1 + gamma^2*r2, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Discounts the immediate reward as well
Drops the third reward entirely
Sums rewards with no discounting

questions.explanation: The discounted return weights each reward by gamma raised to its time index: 8 + 0.9*4 + 0.9^2*8 = 18.08. Summing without discount treats future rewards as equal to immediate ones, dropping the last term truncates the horizon, and applying gamma to the first reward discounts the immediate reward, which the definition does not do.
questions.hint: Raise gamma to the power of each reward's time index before summing.

questions.learningObjective: Apply term weighting to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Suppose the values are 8, 63, and 9; a term appears 8 times in a document. In a corpus of 63 documents it appears in 9 documents. Using tf-idf with natural-log inverse document frequency idf = ln(N/df), what is the term's tf-idf weight in this document, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Omits the logarithm in the idf factor
Reports inverse document frequency alone, ignoring term frequency
Uses a base-ten logarithm instead of the natural logarithm

questions.explanation: The inverse document frequency is ln(63/9) = 1.9459. Multiplying by the term frequency gives 8 * 1.9459 = 15.5673. A base-ten logarithm changes the scale, idf alone ignores how often the term appears here, and dropping the logarithm produces a ratio far larger than the log-scaled weight.
questions.hint: Compute ln(N/df) first, then multiply by the term frequency.

questions.learningObjective: Apply attention to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Suppose the values are 1, 4, and 2; a softmax attention head computes unnormalized scores s1 = 4 and s2 = 0 for two keys. What attention weight is assigned to the first key, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, using only the information above.

options.misconception: Reports the weight of the wrong score
Reports the unnormalized exponential
Normalizes raw scores instead of exponentiating them

questions.explanation: Softmax exponentiates each score and normalizes: e^4 / (e^4 + e^0) = 54.5982 / (54.5982 + 1) = 0.982. Normalizing the raw scores ignores the exponential, reporting e^4 alone is unnormalized, and the complementary weight belongs to the second key. Only the softmax of the first score is correct.
questions.hint: Exponentiate both scores, divide the first exponential by their sum.

questions.learningObjective: Apply language model evaluation to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Suppose the values are 4.5, 2; a language model has a cross-entropy of 4.5 bits per token on a held-out corpus. What is its perplexity (base 2), to three decimals? Give the exact answer, showing the key step.

options.misconception: Raises two to H+1 instead of to H
Doubles the entropy rather than exponentiating
Squares the entropy instead of exponentiating it

questions.explanation: Perplexity is defined as 2 raised to the cross-entropy in bits per token: 2^4.5 = 22.627. Squaring or doubling the entropy are not the definition, and using base ten would correspond to entropy measured in nats or decimal digits rather than bits.
questions.hint: Perplexity is two to the power of the per-token cross-entropy in bits.

questions.learningObjective: Apply fairness metrics to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Working from 0.9, 0.5, a binary classifier selects group A at rate 0.9 and group B at rate 0.5. What is the demographic-parity difference between the two groups, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, using only the information above.

options.misconception: Adds the rates instead of taking their difference
Multiplies the two rates rather than differencing them
Reports the ratio of rates instead of their difference

questions.explanation: Demographic parity difference is the absolute gap in positive selection rates: |0.9 - 0.5| = 0.4. A ratio, a product, or a sum of the two rates measures something different from the difference the demographic-parity criterion uses, so each of those is a distinct misreading of the metric.
questions.hint: Take the absolute value of one selection rate minus the other.

questions.learningObjective: Apply data leakage to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the small sampling procedure below, a classifier yields these values. The data leakage question: a practitioner computes feature means and scaling parameters over the entire labeled dataset, and only afterward splits the data into training and test sets, then reports an unusually high test accuracy. What is the most likely flaw in this procedure? State the correct choice, and state the conclusion.

options.text: Overfitting from too few training epochs.
options.misconception: Wrongly attributes the issue to training duration.

options.text: Leakage: test-set statistics influenced the training pipeline.
Class imbalance: one label dominates the dataset.
options.misconception: Wrongly diagnoses label skew, which is not described.

options.text: Underfitting: the model is too simple for the task.
options.misconception: Wrongly blames model capacity instead of information flow.

questions.explanation: Because the scaling statistics were computed before the split, information from the test set leaked into the transformation applied during training. This data leakage inflates test performance because the held-out examples influenced preprocessing. The other options name unrelated problems: model capacity, label distribution, and training duration are not implicated by preprocessing on the full dataset.
questions.hint: Ask whether any test-set information entered the pipeline before the split.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply decision thresholds to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the small sampling procedure below, a classifier gives the following estimate. The decision thresholds question: a probabilistic classifier outputs a score for the positive class. If the decision threshold for predicting positive is raised while the model and data stay fixed, what generally happens to recall and precision? State the correct choice, and state the conclusion.

options.text: Neither metric changes with the threshold.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes threshold and metrics are independent.

options.text: Recall falls while precision tends to rise.
Recall rises while precision tends to fall.
options.misconception: Describes the effect of lowering, not raising, the threshold.

options.text: Both precision and recall rise together.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the two metrics move in the same direction.

questions.explanation: Raising the threshold makes positive predictions harder to earn, so fewer true positives are captured and recall falls. The predictions that remain positive are on average more confident, so precision tends to rise. Lowering the threshold produces the opposite pattern, and the two metrics do trade off, so they cannot both move together or stay fixed in general.
questions.hint: Consider which predictions are relabeled when the cutoff moves upward.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply intelligent agents to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: A performance measure awards +6 points for each correctly filed document, subtracts 2 for each misfiled document, and subtracts 3 for each second of delay. An agent files 5 documents correctly, misfiles 4, and finishes in 5 seconds. What total score does the performance measure assign to this behavior?

options.misconception: Treats delay cost as a reward instead of a penalty
Counts misplaced items as if they were correctly sorted
Adds the misplacement penalty rather than subtracting it

questions.explanation: The measure sums three signed contributions: +6 times 5 correctly filed documents gives 30, minus 2 times 4 misfiles gives -8, and minus 3 times 5 seconds gives -15. The total 30 - 8 - 15 = 7 rewards correctness and penalizes both errors and delay. Adding the delay term, adding the misfiles, or crediting misfiles as correct all invert the intended penalties, so those totals are wrong.
questions.hint: Write each contribution with its sign, then add the three products.

questions.learningObjective: Apply problem formulation to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: On the question about based on the details given, in the problem formulation scenario, a cleaning robot maps a room but cannot observe furniture that family members move after it looks away. Its wheel commands have perfectly predictable effects, yet the room layout keeps changing while it works and positions vary over a continuum. Which set of environment properties best characterizes this task? State the correct choice, based on the details given.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.
Fully observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.
options.misconception: Wrongly grants the agent complete state information.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, static, discrete.
options.misconception: Ignores both passing time and continuous positions.

options.text: Partially observable, stochastic, static, continuous.
options.misconception: Mistakes unseen changes for random action outcomes.

questions.explanation: The robot cannot see every relevant fact, so the environment is partially observable. Actions have perfectly predictable effects, so it is deterministic. The layout changes while the agent deliberates, so it is dynamic. Positions range over a continuum, so it is continuous. Each competing option flips one of these four properties and therefore misdescribes the task.
questions.hint: Check observability, action predictability, change over time, and whether the state space is discrete.

questions.learningObjective: Apply agent designs to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: On the question about based on the details given, in the agent designs scenario, an agent selects each action using only the percept it receives at this instant. It keeps no record of earlier observations and builds no model of how the environment evolves. Which agent design does this description match? State the correct choice, based on the details given.

options.text: A simple reflex agent acting only on the current percept.
A model-based reflex agent tracking hidden state.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the agent maintains any state at all.

options.text: A utility-based agent maximizing expected satisfaction.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes a utility function over outcomes.

options.text: A goal-based agent planning toward a target state.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes explicit goals and lookahead search.

questions.explanation: A simple reflex agent maps the current percept directly to an action through condition-action rules, with no memory or world model. The description explicitly denies stored history and an environment model, ruling out model-based, goal-based, and utility-based designs, each of which needs internal state beyond the present percept.
questions.hint: Ask whether the agent stores anything beyond the percept in front of it.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply heuristics to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Suppose the values are 0, 4, and 5; on a four-connected grid an agent starts at (0, 0) and must reach a goal at (4, 5). Each unit step costs 1 and no obstacles are present. What is the Manhattan-distance heuristic value at the starting state?

options.misconception: Undercounts by assuming the goal square needs no move
Counts only the larger coordinate displacement
Uses the area of the rectangle instead of step distance

questions.explanation: Manhattan distance adds the absolute coordinate differences: |4 - 0| + |5 - 0| = 4 + 5 = 9. Because there are no diagonal moves, this is also the exact optimal path cost. Multiplying coordinates, dropping one step, or keeping only the larger displacement each fails to sum both coordinate gaps and so understates the distance.
questions.hint: Sum the horizontal and vertical separations independently.
